NJ-2026-A1315.s: The bill would change New Jersey’s statewide rules for moving college credits between public colleges and universities. It would expand how credits from associate degrees, dual enrollment, and reverse transfer programs are handled, and it would set up an Ombudsperson in the Office of the Secretary of Higher Education to help with credit transfer issues. The ombudsperson would also collect data, review the agreement, and prepare an annual public report.

NJ-2026-A1406.s: The Attorney General would have to review and update the state policy for investigating human trafficking, if needed. The review would look at whether undercover police should use audio or video recordings, how to control sharing those recordings, and how county prosecutors should be involved from the start of local investigations. It would affect state, county, and town law enforcement and people who are victims of human trafficking.

NJ-2026-A1408.s: The bill would require certain businesses, public places, and transit sites to post human trafficking warning signs in English, Spanish, Chinese, and Korean. It would affect places like bars, airports, bus and rail stations, truck stops, hospitals, hotels, and some job and farm labor sites. A business that does not comply could face a $300 fine for a first offense and $1,000 for later offenses. The change would take effect immediately.

NJ-2026-A1821.s: Health insurance carriers would not be allowed to deny coverage for a nonopioid prescription drug just to favor an opioid drug, or make a patient try an opioid first, when a doctor prescribes the nonopioid drug for acute pain. Carriers that keep a drug list would have to avoid treating approved nonopioid pain drugs worse than opioid or narcotic pain drugs in coverage or cost sharing. The same rule would also apply to certain state employee health plans and Medicaid.

NJ-2026-A2007.s: The bill would require some health care providers to screen for intimate partner violence and would require health care workers to take steps to keep a victim’s medical record from reaching the person who hurt them. It would also let a patient who may be a victim get referrals to other health care professionals when needed. The state would make a list of services and resources for victims available around New Jersey.

NJ-2026-A2054.s: The bill would require the Division of Children’s System of Care to change its rules for family support and respite care for some people under 21 with developmental disabilities. It would set a 12-month approval period, give families a separate bank of respite hours, and require an annual review, while also letting families stay with the same agency after the review. The act would take effect immediately and has passed the Assembly.

NJ-2026-A2163.s: The bill would require the state human trafficking commission to post public warning signs in more places, including nail salons and Motor Vehicle Commission offices, and it keeps the signs required in other listed businesses and public places. The signs would have to be in English and Spanish and include the human trafficking hotline. Businesses that do not post or replace a missing or damaged sign could face a $300 fine for a first offense and $1,000 for later offenses.

NJ-2026-A2210.s: The bill would require nursing assistant and homemaker-home health aide certification tests to be offered in multiple languages. It would cover the Department of Health and the New Jersey Board of Nursing, and the tests would include languages such as English, Spanish, Haitian Creole, Tagalog, Arabic, Gujarati, and French, with more languages added as needed. The act would take effect on the first day of the sixth month after it is enacted.

NJ-2026-A2762.s: The bill would direct the New Jersey Department of Agriculture to promote New Jersey-made liquor, beer, and wine. It also would add a broader meaning of “wine product” to include fermented drinks made from fruits and other approved ingredients, not just grapes. The department would have to consult people in the wine, beer, and liquor industries when it sets up a quality rating system for alcohol products.

NJ-2026-A2772.s: The bill would require the Division of Child Protection and Permanency to create training on suicide screening and crisis response for caseworkers. The training would cover warning signs, how to respond if a child is at risk, and how to work with mental health workers, schools, resource parents, and community supports. It would be part of new caseworker training and ongoing training, and current caseworkers would have to complete it within 24 months of the bill taking effect.

NJ-2026-A3407.s: The bill would bar colleges and other higher education schools from making students who have children buy meal plans, live in campus housing, or pay gym fees. It would affect students with children at those schools. The Secretary of Higher Education would have to issue rules within six months after the bill becomes law to help schools check who qualifies for the exemption.

NJ-2026-A3424.s: The bill would give priority course registration to certain student parents at colleges and other higher education schools. It would also require the Secretary of Higher Education to set rules and standards for checking who qualifies within six months after the bill becomes law. The bill would have to follow all federal and state rules on discrimination and privacy.

NJ-2026-A425.s: The bill would raise fines for retailers that sell tobacco products to people under 21. It would also require license suspension after a violation, and license revocation after a second or later violation, with a way for people to report violations anonymously. The new rules would take effect 180 days after enactment.

NJ-2026-A4740.s: The bill would require people applying for a commercial driver license, and drivers renewing one, to complete human trafficking awareness training. It would have the Attorney General help develop, approve, review, and update the training course and approve who can provide it. Drivers would also have to certify that they finished the training and note the date and approved provider.

NJ-2026-A4796.s: Would expand criminal and civil penalties for human trafficking. It would also add more human trafficking training requirements for law enforcement. The changes would affect people accused of trafficking and police officers.

NJ-2026-A5040.s: The bill would create a Hope Card program for people protected by a final domestic violence restraining order. It would give them a free wallet-size card or secure electronic record with key order details, and it would let courts, police, judges, and court staff use the program with new training. It would also make a yearly state appropriation from the General Fund for the Judiciary and take effect on the first day of the 13th month after it becomes law.

NJ-2026-A5166.s: Municipalities in New Jersey would not be able to require certain site plan approvals just for adding up to five van accessible parking spaces to an existing parking lot or parking structure in a commercial zone. These spaces must meet federal accessible parking standards, and the rule would apply unless the change cuts the number of parking spaces already required in the original plan. The bill would take effect right away.

NJ-2026-A5441.s: The bill would change the timeline for state help that lets NJ FamilyCare and SNAP applicants and recipients report volunteer or community service hours to meet federal rules. It would require the Department of Human Services and the Department of Labor and Workforce Development to share data and track work and volunteer hours, and it affects people using those programs. It would also shift $50,000 to Human Services and $50,000 to Labor from an existing appropriation for the Office of Volunteerism.

NJ-2026-A5713.s: The bill would let hookah lounges operate under set rules in New Jersey if they register with the local health board and meet smoking-area and ventilation requirements. A lounge would have to keep people under 21 out of the smoking area, and it could not allow cannabis or illegal drugs. Municipalities would have to check whether an application is complete within 10 business days and approve or deny a complete application within 30 calendar days.

NJ-2026-A5714.s: The bill would let the Department of Transportation use licensed third-party permit professionals to review and approve certain access permits for State highways, if the department chooses. It would set up a licensing program for these professionals and give them 90 days to act on a complete permit application. It affects people and developers seeking permits to build or open driveways, streets, or highways that connect to a State highway.

NJ-2026-A5715.s: The bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs, with the Attorney General, to study the Statewide Veterans Diversion Program. The study would look at treatment, case management, housing help, county practices, and program numbers for veterans and other eligible service members. The commissioner would then report the findings and any recommended changes within one year, and the act would take effect immediately.

NJ-2026-A5716.s: The Department of Transportation would study pedestrian safety on South Lakeshore Drive in Pemberton Township and work with the township on the study. It would look at speeding, crashes, and pedestrian injuries and deaths, and then send a report with its findings and ideas to reduce those harms. The act would take effect right away and end after the report is sent.

NJ-2026-A5717.s: The Department of Education would have to post special education complaint investigation reports on its website and keep a public database of special education legal decisions. It would also add links to later state or federal court decisions in those cases, and make the database searchable by things like the issue, the school district, and any award or corrective plan. The bill affects parents, school districts, school staff, and others who use special education records.

NJ-2026-A5718.s: The bill would require the Education Commissioner to appoint an outside, neutral investigator for complaints about special education services against the state Education Department or its offices. The investigator would need to review the complaint, let the person who filed it add more information, and let the department respond. A written decision would be due within 60 days and would be final. The law would take effect on the first day of the second month after it is signed.

NJ-2026-A5719.s: The bill would require the Office of Special Education in the Department of Education, or an independent investigator in some cases, to decide what help a student should get after a State complaint finds the student was denied a free appropriate public education. If compensatory education services are needed, the office would set the amount and type of services, while the student’s IEP team would decide how and when they are provided. It would take effect right away and first apply to the next full school year after it is signed into law.

NJ-2026-A5720.s: The bill would require the Education Commissioner to oversee follow-up on certain orders and correction plans issued after special education complaints. It would affect school districts and other public or private education agencies that serve students with disabilities, and it would also require reports to the commissioner and the person who filed the complaint. If a school or agency still does not comply, the commissioner would have to give notice and could use enforcement steps such as extra monitoring, training, fund limits, payment holds, or referral to the Attorney General.

NJ-2026-A5721.s: The bill would require the State Board of Education to set rules for how the Office of Special Education handles special education complaints. It would require more sharing of documents with the person who filed the complaint, a chance to respond, and a fuller report that lists the evidence used. It would also require public posting of the complaint guide and a form for parents or guardians to ask for help enforcing a corrective action plan, and it would add data tracking to show when each noncompliance problem is fixed.

NJ-2026-A5722.s: The bill would require hotels and harm reduction service providers to work together to provide opioid antidotes, such as naloxone, and harm reduction supplies at hotels. It would let hotels connect with registered harm reduction groups to hand out these supplies and train hotel staff on how to use opioid antidotes. The Health Department would also have to help link harm reduction services with hotels and hotel staff.

NJ-2026-A5723.s: The bill would have the Treasury Department transfer the state’s interest in the Arthur Brisbane Child Treatment Center property in Wall Township to the Department of Environmental Protection. The land is about 386 acres and includes a main house, two cottages, and a school building. The Parks and Forestry division would be in charge, and the property would be kept as open space. It would take effect right away.

NJ-2026-A5724.s: The bill would give certain New Jersey residents a state income tax credit for part of their work-related child care costs for a dependent under age 13. The credit would be limited to taxpayers with New Jersey taxable income of $300,000 or less, with rates that drop as income rises, and it could not be more than $5,000 per child each year. A taxpayer could not use the same expenses for both this credit and the existing state dependent care credit.

NJ-2026-A5725.s: The bill would repeal a 2026 state rule that limits state and local police cooperation with federal civil immigration authorities. It would create a grant program in the Department of Law and Public Safety to help police agencies enter into, renew, or expand certain federal immigration agreements, and it would require a yearly report on the program. The Legislature would be allowed to provide money for the program, and the bill would take effect right away.

NJ-2026-A5726.s: The bill would direct the Board of Public Utilities to set up a competitive process to award incentives for building micro nuclear reactors in New Jersey. It would let the board seek proposals from projects that start after the bill takes effect and connect to a New Jersey power system or serve only New Jersey facilities. The bill also sets rules for bidding, worker pay during construction, and a report to lawmakers within four years after the law takes effect.

NJ-2026-A5727.s: The bill would require the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to let micro-reactors be built and run in the state. Micro-reactors are advanced nuclear reactors that make 20 megawatts or less of power. The reactor design would need approval from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and the act would take effect right away.

NJ-2026-A5728.s: The bill would add voter registration at the same time people apply for a concealed carry handgun permit through local police or the State Police. It would let eligible applicants register to vote, update their voter info, or decline automatic registration. The law would take effect on January 1 after it is enacted.

NJ-2026-A5729.s: State agencies would have to set up faster approval and permit steps for artificial intelligence data centers that use power made on site from natural gas. The Board of Public Utilities, the Department of Community Affairs, and the Department of Environmental Protection would have to make these rules within 12 months after the law takes effect. The rules would also cover faster site review, building plan review, power hookup steps, and some environmental permits.

NJ-2026-A5730.s: The bill would let people in urgent need of insulin get a one-time emergency 30-day supply through a pharmacy, using an application made by the state health insurance department and the Board of Pharmacy. It would apply to New Jersey residents who are not in NJ FamilyCare or a similar program, and who do not have insulin coverage that keeps their out-of-pocket cost at $35 or less for a 30-day supply. Pharmacies could seek payment from the insulin maker or its vendor, and the bill would take effect 180 days after it is enacted.

NJ-2026-A5731.s: The bill would create a two-year pilot program to give county colleges extra state aid for certain noncredit job training programs. These programs would be for short-term workforce needs and may lead to a credential, certification, or license in a high-demand field. It would provide $5 million each year of the pilot from the Workforce Development Partnership Fund.

NJ-2026-A5732.s: This bill would give an extra subsidy for health insurance bought on the state exchange for households with income below 400 percent of the federal poverty level when someone in the home has type 1 diabetes. The money would come from the Health Insurance Affordability Fund, which is already used to help make individual health coverage more affordable. The act would take effect immediately.

NJ-2026-A5733.s: The bill would require the Office of Eviction Prevention to work with the state courts to collect eviction filing data by county and make it public on its website. The data would include counts of landlord-tenant cases, households served with court papers, eviction orders, evictions, and evictions avoided. It would take effect right away.

NJ-2026-A5734.s: State agencies would have to file a notice of intent before starting the formal rulemaking process for a major rule. A major rule is one that could cost more than $10 million a year or at first, or one that could significantly affect local government operations. The rule would apply to State agencies in New Jersey and would take effect 30 days after it is enacted.

NJ-2026-A5735.s: The bill would let New Jersey towns set up seasonal pedestrian malls for a set time of year, with temporary or moveable features. It would allow a town to start studies, then pass an ordinance to create one if the area meets the law’s rules. Owners of land directly next to the proposed mall would get notice before the hearing.

NJ-2026-A5736.s: The bill would require school districts to give students on full school days a lunch period of at least 30 minutes. It would also bar districts from making any student go more than five hours of class time without lunch, and it would not allow lunch to be combined with the required recess period. The rule would not apply to students in half-day programs and would take effect immediately.

NJ-2026-A5737.s: The bill would require the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance to audit payments from drug makers to pharmacy benefits managers and their affiliates. The audited pharmacy benefits manager would pay for the audit and would have 30 days to turn over requested records. If it does not provide the records on time, it could face daily fines of $1,000 to $10,000. The bill would take effect on the first day of the fourth month after it is signed into law.

NJ-2026-A5738.s: The bill would revise New Jersey’s Fair Price Protection Act, which deals with how prices are set for groceries and other food. It would let personal data used for pricing also be used for food safety notices, recall notices, and inventory forecasts, and it would allow some price changes more than once in a day for certain reasons like fixing errors or managing stock. It would also make the Attorney General the only one who can bring a civil case for a violation, require written notice first, and give the person 45 days to fix the problem. The act would take effect right away.

NJ-2026-A5739.s: The bill would temporarily waive fees charged by the state alcohol office for plenary winery, farm winery, and out-of-State winery licenses. It would apply to people or businesses applying for or holding those licenses, and it would cover license, filing, renewal, transfer, salesroom, and other related fees. The waiver would last for the first two full state fiscal years after the bill becomes law and would not end state or federal taxes or municipal fees.

NJ-2026-ACR160.s: This resolution would change New Jersey budget rules to require more disclosure from lawmakers who file budget resolutions. They would have to say what kind of group would get the money, such as a government, for-profit, or nonprofit group, and note if they or close family have ties to that group or got campaign money from its owners, officers, or board members in the past 36 months. It would affect sponsors of budget resolutions and the public record for state budget items.

NJ-2026-AR161.s: The resolution recognizes October as Italian-American Heritage Month in New Jersey. It honors the accomplishments and contributions of Italian Americans to the state and the United States, including in science, business, the arts, sports, public service, and military service. The Assembly passed it and it was filed with the Secretary of State.

NJ-2026-S3546.s: The bill would let mortgage loan originators and certain licensed workers do their job from home or another remote place if they follow written rules for supervision and security. It would apply only when company systems and customer data are handled under a written security plan, no in-person customer meetings happen at a home unless it is a licensed site, and paper records are not kept at the remote site. The Senate passed it, and it then went to the Assembly.

NJ-2026-S4128.s: The bill would require each county college to send acceptance letters to local graduating 12th grade students who live in the county and attend public or nonpublic school. The letter would need to explain how to accept the offer, enroll, register for classes, and get financial aid and student support help. It would also require county college leaders to make guidelines for finding these students and to give a yearly report on the program.

NJ-2026-S687.s: The bill would create a 17-member task force in the Department of Banking and Insurance to study how climate change affects home and business property insurance in New Jersey. Its members would include state officials, lawmakers, private sector representatives, nonprofit members, and academics with climate and insurance knowledge. The task force would review issues like insurance costs, coverage, risk, and access, then submit a report with findings and recommendations within one year after all members are appointed.

NJ-2026-S693.s: Municipalities would not be able to require certain plan approvals for a change that only adds up to five van-accessible parking spaces to an existing parking lot or parking structure in a commercial zone. The rule would apply only when the added spaces meet federal accessibility standards and do not reduce the number of parking spaces required in the original plan. It would take effect right away.
